posts.content: Good objective; with no evidence, each other player is likely good (about 0.71), so cooperate by default. Update beliefs from encounters and act to maximize expected total payoff of good players.
I am good. Against a good player, C benefits the total good-player payoff whether they choose C or D. Against a selfish player, D is better; use C unless selfishness is sufficiently likely.
As a good player, cooperate with likely-good partners; defect when evidence suggests a selfish opponent, since their payoff is excluded from my objective.
Good objective: cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players. Update beliefs from my encounters and treat leader claims as unverified.
Good objective: cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players. Track actions as evidence, remembering a selfish player rationally defects regardless of our move.
Against a likely good player, cooperate to maximize joint welfare; against a likely selfish player, defect. Track observed actions and update beliefs.
Play D every round; it strictly dominates C regardless of opponent’s action. Track observed actions and payoffs for possible repeat encounters.

I’m good. Prior conditioned on my role gives each other player about 0.291 selfish probability. Cooperate with no contrary evidence; track actions and reciprocate cooperation, while defecting against repeated defection.
I’ll choose actions to maximize my payoff; no promises about cooperation. Consider mutual cooperation when it benefits you, but protect yourself against defection.
P10’s public claim of maximizing only personal payoff is evidence of selfishness, though it could be a lie. Against an unobserved opponent, cooperate by default; update from encounter actions.
P6 chose C, strong evidence they are good. P10's message suggests selfishness but is not proof. Favor C against likely-good players; D is better against selfish players, who should choose D.

P10’s message suggests selfishness, though it is not proof. P2 cooperated; no evidence yet about P3. Favor mutual cooperation with likely-good players, and avoid giving a likely-selfish player an easy payoff.

P8 defected against my C; evidence of selfishness, but a good player may retaliate or target perceived selfishness. P10’s public payoff-maximizing stance is a stronger selfishness signal. Keep both beliefs provisional.
P3 chose C; a selfish player strictly prefers D against either action, so treat P3 as good. Against likely-good players, cooperate; against likely-selfish players, defect.

Prior puts each other player near 1/3 selfish. P10 chose D after signaling self-interest; that is evidence, but one encounter is weak. P2 is unobserved; favor C with likely-good opponents and D with likely-selfish ones.
Round 2 vs P1: choose D; it strictly dominates C. My round-1 D earned 5 against P5's C.

P10’s stated self-payoff objective strongly suggests selfish; choose D against them to secure 1 rather than 0 if they defect. P1 defected against my C, evidence of selfishness but only one encounter. Cooperate with likely-good players; update from observed actions.
I’m offering mutual cooperation this round: I’ll choose C, and hope P9 does too.
Selfish objective: choose D in every one-shot encounter; it strictly dominates C. Observed P9 chose C; P8 chose D.

I’m good. P4 and P7 chose C against me, evidence they may be good; P8 is unobserved. For the next action, weigh good-player payoffs and the chance P8 is selfish; a selfish opponent benefits from D, so avoid rewarding likely selfish play.

Observed P6 and P4 choose C against me; this modestly supports them being good. P10’s messages are mixed evidence, not verified. Keep uncertainty about P9; choose to maximize expected welfare of good players.
P5 is untested. Cooperate this round: mutual cooperation with a good player benefits the good-player total more than unilateral defection; update after observing P5.

P6’s C is evidence they’re good; P8’s D is suggestive, not conclusive, since they don’t know my role. P10’s claims are unverified. Against P4, favor C absent evidence they’re selfish; update from their action.

P3 and P5 chose C, so they are good: selfish players strictly prefer D. Cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish ones. P10’s message is an unverified claim, not proof of type.

I’m good, so prioritize mutual cooperation with likely-good opponents; defect when evidence indicates selfishness. P6 is unobserved; update from this encounter and avoid treating one action as conclusive.
Continue choosing D: it strictly dominates C for my payoff. P2 is unobserved; record their action after this round.
P3 is untested; cooperate unless there is evidence they are selfish. Track observed actions and update cautiously.
P1, I’ll cooperate this round. Mutual C gives us 3 each; let’s make it happen.
P10 promised cooperation, then chose D against me; strong evidence P10 is selfish. I will defect in every one-shot encounter.

P1 is unobserved; tentatively cooperate unless new evidence suggests otherwise. P4 and P7 cooperated; P8 defected, which raises suspicion but is not proof. For a good opponent, mutual C maximizes their combined payoff; against a selfish defector, D limits harm to good players.

P4, P6, and P9 chose C against me, strong evidence they are good. Given those observations, selfishness among the remaining players is still plausible; P10’s promises are unverified. Against P8, cooperate only if selfishness is unlikely enough to favor good-player welfare.

P2, P3, and P5 cooperated against me, strongly indicating they are good if selfish players optimize payoff. P10’s self-focused message is suspicious but not proof. Against untested P7, cooperate unless new evidence suggests otherwise.

P10’s stated payoff-maximizing objective and repeated unverified cooperation offers keep selfishness probability high. Against a likely selfish opponent, choose D; update after observing the encounter.

P3, P5, and P7 chose C, strongly indicating they are good. Treat P10’s promises as unverified. For P9, cooperate if likely good; defect if likely selfish, prioritizing the cumulative payoff of good players.

P6 and P10’s observed D against C strongly suggests selfishness; P2’s C suggests good. P4 is unobserved: cooperate unless evidence indicates selfishness. Selfish players favor D; good players generally favor C with one another.
Round 4 vs P3: choose D, which strictly dominates C for my payoff. Record P3’s action and payoff; assess future interaction accordingly.

P6 is untested; lean C to support mutual gains. P1 defected against my C, but one encounter is limited evidence. P10 openly claimed to optimize personal payoff; treat its promises cautiously. Update beliefs from observed actions.
P5, I’ll cooperate this round; mutual C earns us 3 each. Please choose C so we can both benefit.
P6 is an unknown one-shot opponent. D maximizes my payoff regardless of their action; choose D.
P1 and P8’s defections raise suspicion; P4 and P7 cooperated. P5 is unobserved, so cooperate absent evidence they’re likely selfish: mutual C maximizes combined good-player payoffs.

P10’s public cooperation invitations are unverified and mixed with its stated payoff-maximizing stance; keep substantial suspicion, but don’t treat claims as evidence of actual actions. P8 defected against me, which is only modest evidence of selfishness. For good-player welfare, C is preferable against good opponents; D can protect my payoff against selfish D-players.

P2, P3, P5, and P7 all chose C against me, evidence favoring good. P10’s self-focused public statements suggest selfishness but are not proof. P8 is untested; cooperate unless new evidence suggests otherwise, then update from the encounter.
P2 is untested; favor C unless new evidence suggests high selfishness. Good players benefit from mutual cooperation. Keep P8/P10 suspicions provisional and update from observed actions.

P3, P5, P7, and P9 have chosen C, strong evidence they are good. Selfish players strictly prefer D against either action. Treat unobserved players and P10’s promises as uncertain; cooperate with likely-good opponents to support good players’ combined payoff.
P6’s D against my C is evidence of selfishness, though not conclusive. P10’s D after my D is weak evidence. P9 is unobserved; favor C unless new evidence suggests otherwise.
Known selfish; choose D for payoff. Observed: P5, P2, P3 chose C; P1 chose D. Keep tracking opponents’ actions; no claims from others alter incentives.

P7 is untested; lean C to support mutual gains if they are good. P1 defected against my C, while P10 openly claimed a self-payoff objective; treat both as suspect. P3 and P6 cooperated, but one encounter is limited evidence.
P3, I’ll cooperate this round. Mutual C gives us 3 each—please choose C.
I am selfish; D strictly dominates C in every one-shot encounter. P10’s public cooperation offers are cheap talk; my only observation is they chose D against me.

P3 is unobserved; cooperate by default to support mutual gains among good players. P1 and P8 defected, while P4, P5, and P7 cooperated; update identity beliefs cautiously, since actions are evidence, not proof.

For good-player welfare, C is preferable against a good opponent; against a selfish payoff-maximizer, D is safer. P2 is unobserved. P8’s D and P10’s D are weak evidence of selfishness; past C choices are evidence, not proof. Keep uncertainty and choose for expected welfare.
P2, P3, P5, and P7 cooperated against me, strongly favoring good; P8’s defection is evidence of selfishness. P1 is untested: cooperate unless new evidence arrives, then update from the encounter.

P9 is untested; favor C unless new evidence suggests selfishness. P8’s D and P10’s repeated public offers are suggestive, not conclusive. Keep updating cautiously from encounters and remember good players benefit most from mutual C.

P1 chose D against my C, strong evidence they are selfish. P3, P5, P7, P9 chose C and are good under payoff-maximizing play. P10’s repeated promises are not verified; assess its action history cautiously.

P6’s D against my C is strong evidence of selfishness; P2, P4, and P9 cooperated, modest evidence they are good. P10’s mutual D is ambiguous. P8 is unobserved: favor C unless new evidence changes the welfare calculation.
P7, I’ll choose C this round. Mutual cooperation earns us 3 each—please choose C.

Round 6: P1 defected against my cooperation; P10 claimed to maximize personal payoff, both suspicious. P3, P6, and P7 cooperated with me. P5 is untested; lean C to support mutual gains, updating after the encounter.
P6, I'll cooperate this round; choosing C lets us both get 3. Please reciprocate.
I am selfish; in this one-shot encounter D strictly dominates C regardless of P7’s action. Choose D.

P6 is unobserved; P10’s promise to cooperate with P6 is unverified and gives little evidence about P6’s type. Choose based on the expected payoff to all good players, updating cautiously from any new encounter evidence.

P5 is unobserved. Given my good role, the prior implies about 0.407 selfish probability per other player; past C/D behavior is evidence, not certainty. Choose C if P5 likely good, D if likely selfish; P10's promises are unverified.

P1 and P8 defected against my cooperation, making selfishness more likely; P2, P3, P5, and P7 cooperated. P10’s self-payoff framing remains suspicious despite cooperative promises. Against P10, weigh likely defection heavily; update from the encounter.
P3 is untested; favor C to enable mutual cooperation if they’re good. Prior encounters: P6, P4, P2, P9 chose C; P8 chose D; P10 chose D. Treat single actions and public claims as imperfect evidence.

P3, P5, P7, P9 chose C, so they are good; P1 and P10 chose D, so they are selfish. P2, P4, P8 remain uncertain. Against P2, C supports good players’ joint payoff if they are good; D protects against a selfish opponent.
P1 is unobserved; absent contrary evidence, cooperate to support welfare if they are good. Keep P6’s defection against my C as evidence of selfishness; P10’s promises remain unverified.
Known selfish; choose D. P2, P3, P5 chose C, so they are good. P1 and P7 chose D; this alone doesn’t reveal their roles. Reassess remaining players using the count prior.
P8 is untested; lean C to support mutual gains if they are good. P1 defected against my C and P10 claimed to maximize personal payoff, so treat both as suspicious. Update from each encounter.
P4, I’ll choose C this round. Mutual cooperation gives us 3 each—please reciprocate.
I am selfish; in every one-shot encounter, D strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of the opponent’s action. P5 is still unobserved; choose D.

P9 is unobserved. Favor C when expected gains to good players outweigh the risk of helping a selfish defector; use any new evidence cautiously. P1 and P8 defected against me, while P3, P4, P5, P6, and P7 cooperated. P10’s repeated promises are unverified.

P7 is unobserved; conditioned on my good role, prior selfishness is about 0.29 per opponent. Good-player welfare favors C against a good opponent, even if they D; D only gains 1 against a selfish D-player.
P6 is untested; favor C, since mutual cooperation yields more total payoff if P6 is good. Update suspicion from the encounter.

P1 is untested; favor C to support mutual cooperation among good players. Prior C choices from P2, P3, P4, P6, P9 are encouraging but imperfect evidence; P8’s D and P10’s behavior remain suggestive, not conclusive.

P1 and P10 defected against my C, identifying them as selfish; P2, P3, P5, P7, and P9 chose C, identifying them as good. Given the count prior, exactly one of P4/P8 is selfish, equally likely. Against P4, D is best: it yields 5 whether P4 is good or selfish, while C has lower expected good-player payoff.
P3 remains unobserved; P10’s past promises are unverified and don’t reveal P3’s response. Favor C with P3 unless new evidence suggests selfishness.
I am selfish; choose D to maximize my payoff. P10’s public cooperation claims are unverified, and I have no encounter evidence about P10. Track actual actions, not promises.

P1 and P8 defected against my C; P10 openly claimed to maximize personal payoff. Treat them as strong selfish candidates, but remember the prior allows only 1, 3, or 5 selfish players. P2 is untested; favor C absent contrary evidence.
P8, I’ll choose C this round; mutual cooperation gets 3 each. Please reciprocate.
I am selfish; in this one-shot encounter, D strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of P3’s action. Choose D.

P10 has openly claimed to maximize personal payoff, suggesting selfishness, though its repeated C promises may be strategic or truthful. My evidence: P1/P8 defected; P3–P7 and P9 cooperated. Choose to maximize expected payoffs of good players, not trust claims blindly.
P1 is unobserved; keep substantial uncertainty. Good-player welfare favors C against a good opponent, even if they defect; D only gains against a selfish opponent.

P1, P8, and P10 defected; under payoff-maximizing selfish play, defectors are selfish. P2, P3, P5, P6, and P7 cooperated and are good. Thus the known count is three selfish; P9 is likely good. Cooperate with P9.

P7 is untested; favor C to support mutual cooperation among good players. My encounters: P8 and P10 chose D; P1, P2, P3, P4, P6, and P9 chose C. Treat single actions and public claims as imperfect evidence.

P8 is unobserved. P1/P10 defecting against C suggests selfishness, not certainty; C from P2/P3/P4/P5/P7/P9 is strong good-player evidence. Choose against P8 to maximize good players’ joint payoff; leader claims remain unverified.
P5 is unobserved; favor C absent evidence of selfishness. P1 and P6 defected against my C, while P2, P3, P4, and P9 chose C. These are clues, not certainties.
Choose D against P6 to maximize my payoff; D strictly dominates C regardless of P6’s action.

P1 and P8 defected against my C; P10 claimed to optimize personal payoff and defected against me. P3, P5, P6, P7, and P2 cooperated. P4 is untested; lean C to support mutual gains, and update from this encounter.
P2, I’ll choose C this round. Mutual cooperation gives us 3 each—please reciprocate.
Round 10: D strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of P7’s action; prior messages cannot alter that.
P3 cooperated with me in round 6, so favor C again to support mutual good-player gains. This is the final round; no future reciprocity.

P2 chose C against me in round 6, modest evidence they are good; no new evidence since. P1 defected against me in round 9, but one action is not conclusive. Keep beliefs uncertain; prioritize total welfare of good players.
P5 cooperated against me in round 3, strongly favoring good. Cooperate again to support mutual cooperation and maximize the good players’ total payoff.
P4 and I previously chose C and both benefited. I’ll choose C again; mutual cooperation best supports good players. This is our final encounter.
Final round vs P10, who defected against my C in round 6. This strongly suggests selfishness; if so, D yields me 1 rather than 0 and is better for good players’ total. Choose D.

Final round against P1, who previously defected against my C—meaningful evidence of selfishness. For good-player welfare, choose D if P1 is likely selfish; otherwise C supports mutual cooperation. No future rounds remain.
P9 chose C against my D in round 7. I am selfish and choose D; final-round incentives unchanged.

Final round vs P8, who defected against my C before. Still choose C: if P8 is good and cooperates, mutual C maximizes good-player payoff; against a selfish defector, my action cannot improve good-player payoff.
I defected against your C before, so you should expect D again; choosing D avoids being exploited.

belief_records.strategy: Defect in this one-shot encounter: it maximizes my payoff regardless of the opponent’s action.

Cooperate when the expected benefit to good players outweighs the risk of helping a selfish opponent. Update identity beliefs from encounter evidence and choose actions to maximize good-player payoffs.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good-player welfare; defect when a selfish opponent is sufficiently likely.
Cooperate absent encounter evidence; update beliefs and actions as play reveals opponents’ behavior, aiming to maximize good players’ combined payoffs.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent; update beliefs and actions from encounters, while treating public claims as unverified.
Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize good players’ joint payoff; defect when evidence makes an opponent likely selfish. Treat messages as uncertain evidence.
Defect against P10 given the self-interested message and uncertainty; update beliefs from observed actions and cooperate when expected good-player welfare favors it.
Defect each round: D strictly dominates C for my payoff.
Open with cooperation to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from encounter evidence and adapt to opponents’ actions.

Defect in this one-shot encounter because D strictly dominates C. P9’s observed cooperation rules out selfishness; otherwise retain the conditional prior.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent; update identity beliefs from actions, treating selfish players’ dominant incentive to defect as evidence. Choose to maximize the payoffs of all good players.

Defect against P10 given their stated self-payoff objective; update cautiously from actions and messages, while cooperating with likely-good players to maximize good players’ total payoff.

Defect because it strictly dominates cooperation in this one-shot encounter; P10’s promise does not change that.

Cooperate with the untested opponent to support good players’ collective payoff; treat P8’s defection and P10’s statement as evidence, not proof, and update from encounters.
Defect against an unobserved opponent when the chance they are selfish outweighs the joint-good payoff advantage of mutual cooperation; treat leader claims as uncertain evidence.

Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support mutual cooperation among good players; update beliefs from observed actions, treating P2’s C as evidence of good intent and P10’s D as evidence of selfishness.
Choose D to maximize my payoff; it strictly dominates C regardless of P2’s action.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed actions and messages, and adapt to future evidence.
Defect in this one-time encounter: D gives a higher payoff than C whether P1 chooses C or D. The two observed defections indicate P7 and P9 are selfish; update other beliefs accordingly.
Defect: it strictly dominates cooperation in this one-shot encounter. P9’s cooperation rules out selfishness; P10’s broken promise raises my suspicion, though it is not conclusive.

Cooperate with an unobserved opponent when the expected benefit to good players outweighs the risk of helping a selfish player. Treat P8’s defection and P10’s messages as evidence, while updating from future encounters.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good-player welfare; defect when selfishness is sufficiently likely. The observed C actions strongly support P4, P6, and P9 being good.

Cooperate with an untested opponent: mutual cooperation benefits the good-player total, and current evidence does not make P7 likely selfish. Treat P10’s self-focused message as suggestive, not conclusive.

Defect against a likely-selfish opponent; cooperate with likely-good players to maximize good players’ combined payoff. Update identity beliefs from observed actions and treat messages as unverified evidence.
Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize good players’ joint payoff; defect against likely-selfish players. Treat unverified leader promises as weak evidence.

Cooperate with the unobserved opponent to support mutual cooperation among good players. Update beliefs from observed actions, treating defection as evidence of selfishness but allowing good players to defect strategically.
Choose D to maximize my payoff; it strictly dominates C regardless of P3’s action.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed actions and messages, and adapt to future evidence.

Defect: it maximizes my payoff against either opponent action. P2 and P9’s cooperation rules out selfishness; P10’s broken promise raises suspicion.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support mutual gains among good players. Update identity beliefs from observed actions and messages, allowing for strategic play and deception.
Choose C when expected good-player welfare favors it; defect when a selfish opponent is sufficiently likely. P10’s claims are unverified, while P8’s defection raises suspicion.
Cooperate with untested P8 because mutual cooperation benefits good players; observed cooperation makes P2, P3, P5, and P7 unlikely selfish. Treat P10’s messages as suggestive, not conclusive.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when likely to improve good players’ combined payoff; defect when evidence suggests selfishness. Update from encounters, treating claims as unverified.
Cooperate with P1: the evidence makes them more likely good, and cooperation improves the combined payoff when both players are good. Treat unverified promises as weak evidence.
Cooperate with the unobserved opponent to support mutual cooperation among good players; update beliefs from observed actions, treating defection as evidence but allowing strategic play.
Choose D to maximize my payoff; it strictly dominates C regardless of P4’s action.
Cooperate with untested P7 to support mutual gains if they are good; update beliefs from observed actions and treat P1 and P10 as more suspect.

Defect in this one-time encounter: D pays more than C against either action. Given my known selfish role and four observed defections, the five-selfish-player case is forced; the observed opponents and I account for all five.
Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action in this one-shot encounter. The observed cooperators are ruled out as selfish; retain equal conditional prior beliefs for the others.

Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support mutual gains among good players. Treat observed cooperation as strong evidence of good identity and defections or self-focused messaging as suspicion, not certainty.

Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good-player welfare; defect when facing a sufficiently likely selfish player. P2 is unobserved, so cooperation is preferable under current uncertainty.

Cooperate with untested P1: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and current evidence does not make selfishness more likely than goodness. Treat prior behavior and public claims as uncertain evidence.
Cooperate with untested players to support mutual cooperation among good players; update cautiously from observed actions and treat public claims as unverified.

Cooperate with P10: their promise is unverified, but cooperation supports good players’ combined payoff if they are good. Treat P1’s defection as evidence of selfishness and keep other unobserved players uncertain.

Choose D to maximize my payoff; it strictly dominates C regardless of P7’s action.

Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action in this one-shot encounter. The observed cooperators cannot be selfish; retain symmetric beliefs among the remaining candidates.

Cooperate with an unobserved opponent when that best supports expected good-player payoffs. Treat observed defections as evidence of selfishness and cooperation as evidence of goodness, while allowing for strategic play.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good-player welfare; defect when selfishness is sufficiently likely. P5 is unobserved, so the prior favors cooperation.
Defect against P10 given its self-focused framing and repeated promises that could be bait; observed defections raise suspicion for P1 and P8, while cooperation favors P2, P3, P5, and P7.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual cooperation among good players; update identity beliefs from observed actions and treat public claims as uncertain.
Cooperate with P2: with low selfishness probability, mutual cooperation better supports good players’ joint payoff. Treat observed defections as evidence, not certainty, of selfishness.

Cooperate with unobserved P1 to support welfare if they are good; their selfishness probability is too low to justify defecting. Treat P6’s D against C as evidence of selfishness, while C responses modestly favor good.
Choose D to maximize my payoff; it strictly dominates C regardless of P9’s action.
Cooperate with untested P8 to support mutual gains among good players. Use observed actions and credible objective claims to update beliefs, while avoiding overconfidence from a single encounter.
Defect: it gives a higher payoff than cooperation whether P4 chooses C or D. I assign the four available selfish-player slots among the five opponents previously observed choosing D, symmetrically.
Choose D because it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action by P5. Observed cooperators are ruled out as selfish; retain symmetric beliefs among the remaining candidates.

Cooperate with the unobserved P9 to support mutual gains among good players. Treat observed defections as evidence of selfishness and cooperation as evidence of goodness, while allowing for strategic play and deception.

Cooperate with P7, who is unobserved and more likely good than selfish. Observed cooperation lowers suspicion; P8’s defection and P10’s defection after promising C raise it, but neither proves selfishness.
Cooperate with untested P6: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and selfishness is not sufficiently likely to justify defection. Prior defections raise suspicion of P1, P8, and P10.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual cooperation among good players; update cautiously from observed actions and treat public claims as uncertain.
Cooperate with P4 while they remain more likely good; mutual cooperation benefits good players. Treat P1 and P10’s defections as strong but not conclusive evidence of selfishness.

Choose D to maximize my payoff; it strictly dominates C regardless of P10’s action.
Cooperate with untested P2 to support mutual gains if they are good; defecting is safer against a selfish opponent, so update beliefs from their action and past evidence.
Defect maximizes my payoff against either action in this one-time encounter. Prior D choices are evidence of selfishness; P6’s C is evidence against it.

Defect to maximize my payoff against either action. The six opponents who cooperated cannot be selfish; with no reliable identity signal from defection, keep equal beliefs for the three unobserved-as-cooperators players.
Defect against P10 given its self-focused claim and the risk it will defect despite promising C. Treat prior defections as evidence of selfishness and observed cooperation as evidence of goodness.

Cooperate with P1, who is unobserved and more likely good; cooperation maximizes good-player welfare against a good opponent. Observed defections raise suspicion of P8 and P10, but actions and messages are not conclusive.
Cooperate with likely-good P9 to maximize the good players’ combined payoff; defectors against my cooperation are very likely selfish, while observed cooperators are likely good.
Cooperate with untested P7 to support mutual cooperation among good players; use prior encounters as imperfect identity evidence and treat public claims as unverified.
Cooperate with P8 to support good players’ joint payoff if they are good and willing to cooperate. Treat P1 and P10’s defections as evidence of selfishness, but not certainty.
Cooperate with unobserved P5: mutual cooperation among good players yields the best collective payoff, and the chance P5 is selfish is below the threshold where defection improves expected welfare.
Choose D to maximize my payoff; it strictly dominates C regardless of P6’s action.
Cooperate with untested P4 to support mutual gains if they are good; update identity beliefs from observed actions and treat P1, P8, and P10 as more suspicious.
Defect in this one-time encounter: D pays more than C against either action. The beliefs total five expected selfish players, including me.
Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action. The players who cooperated cannot be selfish; the two remaining candidates have low marginal probabilities under the conditioned prior.
Cooperate with P3 given their prior cooperation and the high expected benefit to good players. Treat repeated defections and P10’s self-focused claim as evidence of selfishness, not certainty.
P2 previously chose C, which is strong evidence they are good. Cooperate to maximize good-player welfare; observed defections raise suspicion but do not prove selfishness.
Cooperate with P5, whose prior cooperation strongly indicates they are good. P1 and P8 defected against my cooperation; P10’s demonstrably false claim is suspicious, but unverified.

Cooperate with P4, whose earlier cooperation is strong evidence they’re good; mutual cooperation maximizes good players’ combined payoff. Treat other action and message evidence as informative but imperfect.
Defect against P10: they defected against my cooperation before, making selfishness likely; D protects the good-player total whether they defect again or cooperate.
Cooperate in the final round to favor good-player welfare; P1’s prior defection raises concern, but the chance they are good still makes cooperation preferable overall.
Choose D to maximize my payoff; P9 previously chose C, so D earns 5.
Defect against P8 given their previous defection against my cooperation; in the final round this protects good-player payoff if they defect, while cooperating would be better only if they cooperate.
